nodes.title: Sender can share an encrypted file and optional note via a capability link
nodes.body: A sender chooses one file, optionally adds a short note, and receives a link they can give to a recipient. The recipient uses the link to recover the original file and note in the browser.

nodes.title: Service never receives or persists plaintext content or key material
nodes.body: The server receives only an opaque drop identifier and ciphertext. It must not receive or store plaintext file content, plaintext notes, decryption keys, or recoverable equivalents. This is the first priority.

nodes.title: Fixed stack: React/TS frontend, Node.js/TS backend, SQLite, one npm repository
nodes.body: All code lives in one npm repository. Dependency installation may use the package registry; the running application and its tests use no external services or runtime network beyond local frontend/backend.

nodes.title: Browser-side encryption using Web Crypto API with authenticated encryption; no custom primitives; no Math.random for security material
nodes.body: All encryption and decryption happen in the browser. The implementation must use the platform Web Crypto API. Authenticated encryption is required. Custom cryptographic primitives and Math.random for security material are prohibited.

nodes.title: Decryption key in URL fragment only; server never receives it in HTTP requests
nodes.body: The decryption capability lives in the URL fragment (#). Browsers do not include fragments in HTTP requests, so the server receives only the opaque drop identifier and encrypted material.

nodes.title: Sender receives a recipient share link and a separate revocation token; revocation authority must not be derivable from the recipient link
nodes.body: Two distinct capabilities are issued at upload time. Possession of the recipient link must not allow an adversary to derive or forge the revocation token.

nodes.title: Every drop has a server-enforced expiry; expired or revoked drops fail retrieval consistently
nodes.body: Expiry is set at upload time and enforced by the server. Once a drop is expired or revoked, all subsequent retrieval attempts fail in the same way regardless of which client issues them.

nodes.title: Wrong/missing capability, tampered ciphertext, nonce, or authenticated metadata must fail closed without exposing partial plaintext or corrupting server state
nodes.body: Any integrity failure at the decryption boundary — bad key, truncated ciphertext, flipped byte, altered AAD — must produce a clean failure, never partial content. Server state must not be corrupted by malformed requests.

nodes.title: Output safety: filenames and notes render as text; no HTML execution in the application origin; path-like filenames must not control server filesystem paths
nodes.body: Filenames and note text are rendered as plain text. Downloads must not execute uploaded HTML in the application origin (content-disposition and content-type controls required). Filename values must be sanitized before use in any server filesystem operation.

nodes.title: Local demo only; running application and tests use no external services or runtime network
nodes.body: The demo runs locally. The running application and its test suite must operate without any external service calls at runtime.

nodes.title: Repository must provide npm test and npm run build; build produces a complete runnable application without ambient dependencies
nodes.body: Both commands are required. npm run build must produce the complete runnable application. No controller-repository files or ambient dependencies may be required.

nodes.title: In-scope threat model
nodes.body: Honest-but-curious service/storage operator; accidental server-side disclosure; guessed drop identifiers; malformed or adversarial clients; stored content injection (XSS via filename or note).

detail.statement: The threat model covers: honest-but-curious service/storage operator, accidental server-side disclosure, guessed identifiers, malformed clients, and stored content injection.

nodes.title: Out-of-scope threat model
nodes.body: Compromised sender or recipient devices; traffic-analysis resistance; denial-of-service resistance beyond simple size limits; formal cryptographic certification.

detail.statement: Out of scope: compromised sender/recipient devices, traffic-analysis resistance, DoS resistance beyond simple size limits, formal cryptographic certification.

nodes.title: Ciphertext envelope schema: single encrypted envelope
nodes.body: The browser serialises file bytes and note text (if present) into one plaintext bundle and encrypts the bundle with one AES-GCM operation. The server stores one ciphertext blob and one nonce. The bundle format must be documented so the recipient client can deserialise correctly.

detail.chosen_option: Single encrypted envelope: one bundle, one AEAD operation, one ciphertext column
rejected: Separate encrypted file and note fields (two ciphertexts, nullable note columns, sub-key derivation required)
detail.rationale: The honest-but-curious threat model warrants hiding even note presence/absence from the server. One AEAD operation with a defined bundle format is simpler to reason about and verify than two operations with domain-separation requirements. Bundle format cost is low for v1 with no backwards-compatibility pressure.

nodes.title: Revocation capability storage: SHA-256 hash of token
nodes.body: The server stores SHA-256(revocation_token) per drop. At revocation time the client presents the raw token; the server hashes and compares. The recipient share link contains only the drop id and decryption key — never the raw token or its hash. No server secret is required.

detail.chosen_option: Store SHA-256(revocation_token) per drop; verify by hashing the presented token at revocation time
rejected: HMAC over drop id with a server secret (requires secret management, breaks zero-config demo, catastrophic on secret leakage)
detail.rationale: High-entropy random tokens make hash storage safe without a salt. No server secret needed, compatible with zero-config local demo, and simple to implement and verify.

nodes.title: Drop identifier and AAD: browser generates UUID v4 before encryption; all five operational fields are bound
nodes.body: Before encryption, the browser generates the drop id with crypto.randomUUID() and selects the expiry timestamp. The AES-GCM encrypt and decrypt operations include all five operational fields as additional authenticated data: drop id, filename, MIME type, file size (bytes), and expiry timestamp. POST /drops carries that same drop id. The server validates canonical UUID v4 syntax, stores the client-supplied id unchanged as the primary key, and returns 409 on collision; it never substitutes an id after encryption. Any server-side modification to an AAD field causes decryption to fail.

detail.chosen_option: Browser-generated UUID v4 before encryption; all five fields bound as AAD; server validates and rejects collisions
rejected: Server-generated id after upload (the browser cannot bind an unknown id into AAD)
Two-step server reservation endpoint (adds a round-trip and lifecycle state without a security benefit)
Drop id + expiry only
Drop id only
detail.rationale: Client generation preserves the single-POST flow and makes the id available before encryption. UUID v4 collision risk is negligible, while server-side validation and primary-key uniqueness preserve the trust boundary. Binding all five fields prevents expiry, filename, MIME-type, size, or cross-drop substitution.

nodes.title: Tooling and test stack: Vite + Vitest + Express + better-sqlite3
nodes.body: React/TS frontend uses Vite as build tool. Vitest is the single test runner and package.json maps npm test to vitest --run. Crypto-envelope tests use real Web Crypto in the Node test environment; React component tests use jsdom and mock the narrow crypto adapter rather than passing cross-realm ArrayBuffer values into real SubtleCrypto. Express integration tests run under Vitest with Supertest. Node.js/TS backend uses Express, and SQLite is accessed via better-sqlite3.

detail.chosen_option: Vite (frontend build) + Vitest (test runner) + Express/Supertest (backend and integration tests) + better-sqlite3 (SQLite driver)
rejected: Create React App (deprecated, slower)
Jest (duplicates Vite transforms and configuration)
Fastify (more setup for minimal gain in demo context)
Hono (less familiar, edge-first)
Drizzle ORM (over-engineering for a small schema)
node:sqlite Node 22 built-in (newer, less documented API)
detail.rationale: Vitest shares Vite's TypeScript transform path and makes npm test actionable from a greenfield repository. Separating real crypto tests from jsdom component tests avoids cross-realm WebCrypto failures. Express is minimal and widely understood; better-sqlite3 suits a single-process demo with deterministic tests.

nodes.title: Resource limits: 10 MB upload ceiling, 24-hour default expiry
nodes.body: The server rejects uploads exceeding 10 MB. The default expiry duration is 24 hours from upload time. Both values are enforced server-side.

rejected: 50 MB / 100 MB ceiling (browser-memory encryption cost, slower tests)
7-day expiry (too relaxed for demo)
1-hour expiry (awkward for real use, though better for testing)
detail.rationale: 10 MB keeps browser memory pressure low and tests fast. 24 hours is long enough for real use in a demo and short enough to demonstrate expiry meaningfully.

nodes.title: Local demo startup: single npm run dev via concurrently
nodes.body: A single npm run dev command starts both the Vite frontend dev server and the Express backend in parallel using the concurrently package. Production mode: npm run build produces a dist/ that the Express server serves as static files; npm start runs the backend only.

detail.chosen_option: Single npm run dev via the concurrently package, starting both Vite and Express in parallel
rejected: Two separate terminal commands (dev:frontend + dev:server)
Build-only spec with no dev mode
detail.rationale: Single-command startup reduces friction for a demo. concurrently is a well-known dev dependency for this pattern.

nodes.title: Project execution harness
nodes.body:
execute.verify: npm test
Test runner contract: package.json script "test": "vitest --run".

nodes.title: Sender shares an encrypted file and optional note via a capability link
nodes.body:
1. Sender opens the application in a browser.
2. Sender selects one file (≤ 10 MB) and optionally types a short note.
3. Before encryption, the browser generates the drop id with crypto.randomUUID(), selects the expiry timestamp, and generates a random AES-GCM key (256-bit) plus 12-byte nonce via Web Crypto API.
4. The browser serialises the file bytes and note text into a bundle and encrypts it; AAD = drop id + filename + MIME type + file size + expiry.
5. The browser uploads the client-generated drop id, ciphertext, nonce, and plaintext AAD fields to the server in one POST.
6. The server validates and stores the drop, returning the same drop id and a raw revocation token; malformed ids fail with 400 and collisions fail with 409.
7. The browser presents the sender with a recipient share link and a separate revocation link.
8. Sender can use the revocation link to delete the drop before expiry.

nodes.title: Recipient recovers the original file and note from a valid capability link
nodes.body:
1. Recipient opens the recipient share link in a browser.
2. The browser extracts the drop id from the path and the decryption key from the URL fragment (never sent to server).
3. The browser fetches ciphertext, nonce, and AAD metadata from the server using the drop id.
4. The browser decrypts using the extracted key, nonce, and server-returned AAD fields.
5. On success: the browser presents the plaintext note as text and offers the file for download with content-disposition: attachment.
6. On failure (wrong key, tampered ciphertext/AAD, expired, revoked): the browser shows an error with no partial content.

nodes.title: Browser generates the drop id before AES-GCM-256 encryption and binds all five operational fields into AAD
nodes.body: The browser generates a UUID v4 drop id with crypto.randomUUID() before encryption. SubtleCrypto.encrypt uses AES-GCM, a 256-bit key, a 12-byte random nonce from crypto.getRandomValues, and AAD composed of the drop id, filename, MIME type, file size, and expiry timestamp serialised deterministically. POST /drops transmits the same drop id, and decryption reconstructs the same AAD from server-returned fields.

given: a file and optional note are ready for upload
a UUID v4 drop id has been generated with crypto.randomUUID()
a 256-bit key and 12-byte nonce have been generated via Web Crypto API
when: the browser calls SubtleCrypto.encrypt with the bundle plaintext and the five-field AAD
then: the client-generated drop id, ciphertext, nonce, and plaintext AAD fields are uploaded in one POST
the plaintext bundle is not transmitted
the key is not transmitted

nodes.title: Decryption key lives in the URL fragment only; no HTTP request transmits it
nodes.body: The recipient link encodes the raw key as base64url in the URL fragment. The server never receives, logs, or stores key material.

given: a recipient share link has been generated
when: the recipient browser opens the link and fetches drop metadata
then: the HTTP request contains the drop id path segment only
the URL fragment is not sent to the server
the server response contains ciphertext and AAD fields only

nodes.title: Server rejects uploads exceeding 10 MB with a 413 response
nodes.body: The server enforces a 10 MB limit on the total upload payload. Requests exceeding this limit receive a 413 before the body is processed. No drop is created.

given: a client attempts to upload a drop
when: the total request body exceeds 10 MB
then: the server responds 413
no drop is created
no data is persisted

nodes.title: Server enforces 24-hour expiry; retrieval of an expired drop returns 404 or 410
nodes.body: Every drop has an expiry timestamp set to 24 hours after upload. The server checks expiry on every retrieval. Expired drops return 404 or 410.

given: a drop whose expiry timestamp is in the past
then: the server responds 404 or 410
no ciphertext is returned

nodes.title: Revocation marks the drop deleted; token verified via SHA-256 hash; subsequent retrieval fails
nodes.body: A DELETE to the revocation endpoint with the raw token causes the server to hash it, compare against the stored hash, and on match mark the drop revoked. Subsequent retrieval returns 404 or 410. The raw token is never stored.

given: a valid drop exists
the sender possesses the revocation token
when: the sender sends a DELETE request with the raw revocation token
then: the server verifies SHA-256(token) against the stored hash
the drop is marked revoked
subsequent retrieval returns 404 or 410

nodes.title: Decryption fails closed on wrong key, tampered ciphertext, nonce, or AAD; no partial plaintext is exposed
nodes.body: SubtleCrypto.decrypt throws on any integrity failure. The application clears intermediate state and shows only a generic failure message.

given: the recipient browser has fetched ciphertext and AAD from the server
when: decryption is attempted with a wrong key, truncated ciphertext, flipped byte, or altered AAD
then: SubtleCrypto.decrypt throws
no plaintext content is rendered
no partial file bytes are exposed

nodes.title: Filenames and notes render as text; downloads force attachment; filenames sanitized server-side
nodes.body: Notes are displayed in a plain-text element. Filenames are displayed as text. The server sets Content-Disposition: attachment on download responses. Filename values are sanitized (path separators removed, length bounded) before any server-side use.

nodes.title: Crypto envelope module (browser)
nodes.body:
Browser-only TypeScript module responsible for:
- Key generation: SubtleCrypto.generateKey (AES-GCM, 256-bit).
- Nonce generation: crypto.getRandomValues, 12 bytes.
- Bundle serialisation: 4-byte big-endian note-length prefix, UTF-8 note bytes, then file bytes.
- Encrypt: SubtleCrypto.encrypt(AES-GCM, key, bundle, { iv: nonce, additionalData: aad }).
- Decrypt: SubtleCrypto.decrypt; deserialise bundle.
- AAD encoding: deterministic serialisation of drop id + filename + MIME type + file size + expiry.
- Key transport: base64url encode/decode for URL fragment.
- No Node.js APIs; no server imports.

nodes.title: Backend API module (Express + SQLite)
nodes.body:
Node.js/TypeScript Express server responsible for:
- 10 MB upload ceiling enforced before body processing.
- Validating the client-supplied drop id as canonical UUID v4, storing it unchanged, returning 400 for malformed ids and 409 for primary-key collisions.
- Generating only the raw revocation token via crypto.randomBytes.
- Storing SHA-256(revocation_token) per drop; never storing the raw token.
- SQLite schema (better-sqlite3): drops table — id TEXT PK, ciphertext BLOB, nonce BLOB, filename TEXT, mime_type TEXT, file_size INTEGER, expires_at INTEGER (Unix ms), revocation_hash TEXT, revoked INTEGER DEFAULT 0, created_at INTEGER.
- GET /drops/:id: check expires_at and revoked before returning ciphertext + nonce + AAD fields.
- DELETE /drops/:id: verify SHA-256(presented_token) = stored hash; set revoked = 1.
- Content-Disposition: attachment on download responses.
- Filename sanitisation: strip path separators, bound length to 255 bytes.
- Serve Vite dist/ as static files in production.

nodes.title: Frontend sender module (React)
nodes.body:
React/TypeScript sender-flow components:
- File picker (single file, client-side 10 MB pre-check).
- Note textarea (plain text).
- Upload button: generates drop id with crypto.randomUUID() and selects expiry before calling the crypto envelope module, then POSTs the id and encrypted envelope to /drops.
- Result view: copiable recipient link and revocation link.
- Revocation action: DELETE /drops/:id; confirmation message.
- Error states for malformed request, id collision, upload failure, and revocation failure.

nodes.title: Frontend recipient module (React)
nodes.body:
React/TypeScript recipient-flow components:
- On mount: extract drop id from URL path, key from URL fragment.
- Fetch GET /drops/:id.
- Call crypto envelope module to decrypt.
- Success: render note as plain text; Download button (Blob URL, content-disposition attachment, original filename).
- Failure: generic error message; clear all in-memory material.
- Fragment must not be forwarded in any request or logged.

nodes.title: Drop API
nodes.body:
POST /drops
  Body: { dropId: UUIDv4, ciphertext: base64, nonce: base64, filename: string, mimeType: string, fileSize: number, expiresAt: ISO8601 }
  Response 201: { dropId: string, revocationToken: string }
  Response 400: malformed request or non-canonical/non-v4 drop id
  Response 409: drop id already exists
  Response 413: payload exceeds 10 MB

GET /drops/:id
  Response 200: { ciphertext: base64, nonce: base64, filename: string, mimeType: string, fileSize: number, expiresAt: ISO8601 }
  Response 404/410: not found, expired, or revoked

DELETE /drops/:id
  Body: { revocationToken: string }
  Response 204: revoked
  Response 401: token mismatch
  Response 404: drop not found

nodes.title: Plaintext sentinel absent from SQLite, server logs, and captured HTTP traffic after upload
nodes.body: A deterministic fixture file contains a unique plaintext sentinel string. After upload, the sentinel must not appear in any SQLite column, server log, or captured request/response body.

given: a fixture file containing a unique plaintext sentinel string
when: the file is encrypted and uploaded via the sender flow
then: the sentinel does not appear in any SQLite column
the sentinel does not appear in server log output
the sentinel does not appear in any captured HTTP request or response body

nodes.title: Recipient recovers byte-identical file and exact note after a valid upload-download cycle
nodes.body: Decrypted file bytes must be identical to the original fixture file bytes; decrypted note must equal the original note string.

given: a fixture file with known content and a known note string
when: the file and note are encrypted, uploaded, then decrypted by the recipient flow
then: decrypted file bytes are identical to the fixture bytes
decrypted note equals the known note string

nodes.title: GET after expiry returns 404 or 410 with no ciphertext; verified with controlled clock
nodes.body: The test suite injects a controlled clock. Advancing past the expiry timestamp causes GET /drops/:id to return 404 or 410 with no ciphertext field.

given: a drop with expiry T has been uploaded
the server clock is advanced past T
then: the server responds 404 or 410
no ciphertext field is present in the response

nodes.title: GET after valid DELETE returns 404 or 410; recipient link alone cannot revoke
nodes.body: DELETE with correct token returns 204; subsequent GET returns 404/410. DELETE with only the recipient link data (no revocation token) returns 401.

given: a valid drop exists
when: DELETE /drops/:id with the correct revocation token is sent, then GET /drops/:id is sent
then: DELETE returns 204
subsequent GET returns 404 or 410

nodes.title: Tampered ciphertext, nonce, or AAD field causes decrypt to throw; no partial content rendered
nodes.body: Each tamper case (one flipped byte in ciphertext; altered nonce; changed AAD field) must cause SubtleCrypto.decrypt to throw and the UI to show only a generic error.

given: a valid drop has been uploaded
when: one byte of ciphertext, the nonce, or an AAD field is altered before decrypt
then: SubtleCrypto.decrypt throws
no plaintext content is rendered
the UI shows a generic failure message

nodes.title: Upload of 10 MB + 1 byte returns 413; no drop row created
nodes.body: POST /drops with a 10 MB + 1 byte body must return 413. The drops table must contain no new row.

given: the server is running
when: POST /drops is sent with a body of 10 MB + 1 byte
then: the server responds 413
the drops table contains no new row

nodes.title: URL fragment (decryption key) does not appear in any captured HTTP request to the server
nodes.body: All HTTP requests made during a full recipient flow are captured. No request URL, header, or body contains the base64url key string from the fragment.

given: a valid share link with the key in the URL fragment
when: the recipient flow fetches and decrypts the drop
then: no captured HTTP request to the server contains the key string in URL, headers, or body

nodes.title: Secure Drop v1
nodes.body:
Entry: all REQ1–REQ7 settled, VV1 execution harness confirmed.
Exit: npm test passes, npm run build produces a runnable application.

nodes.title: Scope: Crypto envelope
nodes.body:
Implements the browser-side crypto envelope module (d-mod-crypto):
- Bundle serialisation / deserialisation.
- AES-GCM-256 key + nonce generation.
- SubtleCrypto.encrypt / SubtleCrypto.decrypt with five-field AAD supplied by the caller, including the already-generated drop id.
- Base64url key transport.
- Vitest unit tests with real Node Web Crypto: round-trip byte-identity, tamper detection per AAD field, wrong-key rejection.

No server dependency. Can be built and tested independently.

nodes.title: Scope: Backend core
nodes.body:
Implements the Express server and SQLite persistence (d-mod-backend):
- Schema, migrations (better-sqlite3 synchronous DDL).
- POST /drops validates and stores the client-generated UUID v4; malformed ids return 400 and collisions return 409.
- GET /drops/:id and DELETE /drops/:id.
- Expiry and revocation enforcement.
- 10 MB ceiling, filename sanitisation, Content-Disposition.
- Controlled clock injection for expiry tests.
- Vitest + Supertest integration tests for server-level acceptance criteria, including UUID validation and collision handling.

Requires stable AAD field contract from Scope: Crypto envelope.

nodes.title: Scope: Frontend sender flow
nodes.body:
Implements d-mod-sender:
- File picker, note textarea, Upload button.
- Client-side 10 MB pre-check.
- Generate UUID v4 drop id and select expiry before encryption.
- Encrypt via Scope: Crypto envelope module API; POST the same id and envelope to Scope: Backend core.
- Display recipient link and revocation link.
- Revocation action.
- Vitest/jsdom component tests mock the narrow crypto adapter; real Web Crypto remains covered by the crypto-envelope scope.

Depends on: Scope: Crypto envelope (module API stable), Scope: Backend core (API contract stable).

nodes.title: Scope: Frontend recipient flow
nodes.body:
Implements d-mod-recipient:
- Extract drop id from path, key from fragment.
- Fetch from Scope: Backend core; decrypt via Scope: Crypto envelope.
- Note as plain text; Download via Blob URL.
- Generic error view.

Depends on: Scope: Crypto envelope (module API stable), Scope: Backend core (API contract stable).

nodes.title: Scope: End-to-end verification
nodes.body:
Implements the full Vitest suite targeting npm test (vitest --run):
- Deterministic fixture files with unique plaintext sentinels.
- Full upload-download round-trip (byte-identical + exact note).
- Client-generated drop id is identical in POST body, stored row, response, share link, and decrypted AAD.
- Malformed/non-v4 ids return 400; duplicate ids return 409 without replacing the stored row.
- Sentinel absence check (SQLite, logs, requests).
- Expiry enforcement (controlled clock).
- Revocation enforcement.
- Tamper tests (ciphertext, nonce, each of five AAD fields).
- 413 on oversized upload.
- Fragment not-sent verification (request capture).
- Build verification: npm run build produces a servable dist/.

Depends on: all prior scopes.

nodes.title: Sender and recipient UI present capability links, decrypted note, and file download as accessible plain-text controls
nodes.body: The sender flow displays the recipient share link and revocation link as copiable plain text. The recipient flow renders the decrypted note as plain text and offers the decrypted file via a Download control. Both flows expose accessible labels on all interactive controls and show only generic error text on failure.

nodes.title: Scope: Frontend (sender + recipient)
nodes.body:
Merged scope implementing both the sender flow (MOD3) and recipient flow (MOD4):
- Sender: file picker, note textarea, client-side 10 MB pre-check, UUID v4 generation before encryption, upload orchestration via the crypto envelope module, result view with copiable recipient and revocation links, revocation action.
- Recipient: fragment/drop-id extraction, fetch via the Drop API, decryption via the crypto envelope module, plain-text note render, Blob-URL download, generic failure display.
- Fragment (decryption key) is never forwarded in any request from either flow.
- Vitest/jsdom component tests mock the crypto adapter; crypto-envelope tests exercise real Web Crypto separately.

Depends on: Scope: Crypto envelope (module API stable), Scope: Backend core (API contract stable).

nodes.title: Project execution harness
nodes.body:
execute.setup: npm install
execute.build: npm run build
execute.verify: npm test
Test runner contract: package.json script "test": "vitest --run".

nodes.title: Repository must include a .gitignore excluding node_modules, dist, and other generated build artifacts from version control
nodes.body: The first slice to initialize the repository must create a .gitignore covering node_modules/, dist/, build/, and any generated test-runner cache directories (e.g. .vite/). This prevents regenerated, non-deterministic package and cache content from being tracked in git and causing merge conflicts during slice integration across independently-run npm install invocations.

nodes.title: CSS approach: plain CSS modules
nodes.body: Visual styling uses plain CSS modules (per-component scoped .module.css files), added via Vite's built-in CSS Modules support. No additional runtime or build-time styling dependency.

detail.chosen_option: Plain CSS modules (Vite built-in support, no extra dependency)
rejected: Tailwind CSS (adds a build-time dependency)
CSS-in-JS / styled-components (adds a runtime dependency)
detail.rationale: Keeps the dependency surface minimal for a bounded demo. Vite supports CSS Modules natively with zero configuration.

nodes.title: Sender and recipient UI present a coherent visual design with distinct interaction states
nodes.body: The sender and recipient views share a consistent visual system (spacing, typography, color) via plain CSS modules. Upload and decrypt operations show a visible loading/in-progress state. Success and failure states are visually distinct (background/icon/border treatment) while error copy remains generic per REQ6. The recipient link and revocation link are visually distinguished from each other so the sender cannot confuse which to share. Recipient/revocation links include a copy-to-clipboard button with visible confirmation feedback. The layout is responsive across desktop and mobile viewport widths.

nodes.title: Visual states are distinct and interactive; recipient/revocation links are visually distinguished with working copy-to-clipboard
nodes.body: Automated test asserts: a loading indicator is present during upload/decrypt async operations; success and failure states apply visually distinct CSS classes; the recipient link container and revocation link container have distinguishing visual treatment (e.g. different container class/label); clicking each link's copy button copies the correct string and shows a confirmation.

given: a completed upload producing a recipient link and a revocation link
when: the sender views the result screen and clicks each copy button
then: the recipient link and revocation link containers carry visually distinguishing classes
each copy button copies its own correct link string
a visible confirmation appears after each copy action

nodes.title: Vite dev server proxies API requests to the Express backend during npm run dev
nodes.body: vite.config.ts must configure server.proxy so that /drops (and any other backend API path prefix) is forwarded from the Vite dev server (port 5173) to the Express backend (port 3001, or process.env.PORT if set). Without this, npm run dev serves the frontend and backend on separate origins with no routing between them, causing all API calls from the browser to 404 against Vite's dev server instead of reaching Express. Production mode (npm run build && npm start) is unaffected since Express serves both the built frontend and the API from one origin.

detail.chosen_option: Configure vite.config.ts server.proxy to forward API path prefixes (e.g. /drops) to http://localhost:3001 (or process.env.PORT) during npm run dev
rejected: Requiring the frontend to call an absolute backend URL directly (breaks the same-origin assumption used in production and complicates CORS)
Leaving dev-mode API calls broken and only supporting the built/production path
detail.rationale: npm run dev is the documented local demo entry point (D6, CON9) and must actually work end-to-end; a missing dev proxy silently breaks every API call from the browser while unit/integration tests (which call the Express app directly via supertest, bypassing Vite entirely) never exercise this path.

nodes.title: npm run dev serves a working end-to-end application: browser requests to /drops reach the Express backend through the Vite dev server
nodes.body: vite.config.ts configures server.proxy to forward /drops (and any other backend route prefix) from the Vite dev server to the Express backend's port. A POST to /drops issued by the browser while npm run dev is running must reach the Express handler and receive the same response it would in production, not a 404 from the Vite dev server.

given: npm run dev is running (Vite dev server and Express backend both started via concurrently)
when: the browser issues a fetch to /drops or /drops/:id from a page served by the Vite dev server
then: the request is proxied to the Express backend and returns the same response the backend would give directly
the response is not a 404 from the Vite dev server itself

nodes.title: Product name: Wisp
nodes.body: The application remains branded as "Wisp" throughout the terminal shell and page title. The canonical fixture slug is "wisp-secure-drop" so the reusable seed is self-describing without changing the product's established identity.

rejected: Secure Drop (generic working title, not a product name)
Wisp Secure Drop (useful as a fixture description, but unnecessarily expands the product name)
Literal/descriptive names (e.g. CipherDrop, VaultShare) — less connected to the established Wisp identity
detail.rationale: Wisp stays short, memorable, and on-theme; the separate wisp-secure-drop fixture slug provides repository-level clarity.

nodes.title: Application uses a shared secure-terminal shell across sender and recipient views
nodes.body: Both routes render a dark, command-line-inspired shell branded "Wisp": a monospace interface, green-on-near-black palette, subtle terminal borders, prompt-style labels, timestamped local-status lines, and a persistent security/status strip. The sender route presents file selection, optional note, expiry, local encryption progress, and drop creation as one terminal session. The recipient route presents capability recovery, ciphertext retrieval, local authentication/decryption status, file metadata, and download as the corresponding receive session. Cryptographic state is legible but not exposed as configurable controls. The shell is keyboard-first, responsive, uses visible focus, announces status changes accessibly, renders user content as text, and sets the page title to the product name.

nodes.title: Secure-terminal shell renders consistently and accessibly across sender and recipient routes
nodes.body: Automated tests assert that both routes use the Wisp terminal shell, expose route-appropriate local security events and actions, preserve keyboard and screen-reader behavior, and set the product page title.

given: the application is rendered at the sender route and, separately, at a recipient route
when: the page shell mounts and the active workflow changes state
then: both routes render the same dark monospace terminal frame with a Wisp prompt label and persistent security/status strip
the sender route exposes local encryption events plus command-styled file, note, expiry, and create-drop controls
the recipient route exposes capability, retrieval, authentication, and decryption events plus a command-styled download action
status changes are announced without moving focus, all actions remain keyboard operable with visible focus, and user-controlled filenames and notes render as text
document.title contains Wisp

nodes.title: Server time is injectable: backend takes a now() dependency
nodes.body: The Express/SQLite backend never calls Date.now() directly. Expiry computation and expiry evaluation both read a clock dependency supplied at construction. Production wires the real clock; tests supply a fake that can be advanced past a drop's expires_at without touching global time or writing rows by hand.

detail.chosen_option: Injectable clock: the backend accepts a now() dependency; tests pass a fake.
rejected: Vitest fake timers wrapping the real Date — awkward against better-sqlite3 and any SQL-side time comparison, and leaves no explicit seam in design.
Tests write a past expires_at directly into SQLite — exercises retrieval but bypasses expiry computation entirely.
Test-only time offset honoured by the server — puts test-only behaviour into production code paths.
detail.rationale: AC3 requires expiry verified with a controlled clock. An explicit seam makes both the computation path (24-hour default from D5) and the evaluation path testable, and keeps test control out of production branches.

nodes.title: Traffic-capture oracle is a server-side request recorder
nodes.body: Verification of what the service actually received is performed by a test-only recorder mounted ahead of the API routes, capturing method, URL (including query string), headers, and raw body for every request. This recorder is the single subject of any claim about captured HTTP traffic.

detail.chosen_option: Server-side test-only recorder capturing method, URL, headers, and raw body for every request.
rejected: Browser-side fetch spy in jsdom — observes attempts rather than what the server received.
Both recorder and fetch spy cross-checked — rejected for now; adds a second oracle surface.
Assert only on requests the test itself issues via supertest — cannot observe requests made by application code.
detail.rationale: AC1's claim is about what reached and persisted on the server, which the recorder observes directly. Chosen despite the known weakness that AC7's negative claim about the URL fragment is only partially probed by a server-side view.

nodes.title: Real AES-GCM is exercised in a node-environment Vitest suite
nodes.body: Crypto-envelope verification runs in a Vitest suite configured with the node environment, using Node's built-in webcrypto as the SubtleCrypto provider. Component suites remain in jsdom with the crypto adapter mocked, per SCP6. No browser engine is required by npm test.

detail.chosen_option: Node-environment Vitest suite using Node's webcrypto.
rejected: jsdom suite with Node webcrypto injected as globalThis.crypto — global patching obscures which implementation is under test.
Vitest browser mode against a real browser engine — introduces an ambient dependency, conflicting with CON8 and CON9.
detail.rationale: AC2 and AC5 need genuine authenticated encryption semantics. Node's webcrypto is the same Web Crypto API surface CON2 mandates, available with no external service or downloaded browser.

nodes.title: Automated axe-core scan is the UI acceptance standard
nodes.body: UI acceptance evidence is an axe-core scan of the rendered sender and recipient views reporting zero serious or critical violations. Role/label queries, per-state CSS-module class assertions, clipboard stubs, and DOM snapshots are not adopted as acceptance standards.

detail.chosen_option: Automated axe-core scan with zero serious violations as the sole automated UI acceptance standard.
rejected: Role/label/ARIA assertions via testing-library queries.
Per-state distinct CSS-module class assertions.
Clipboard stub asserting copy writes the correct link.
DOM snapshots of the shell across both routes.
Documented manual checklist.
detail.rationale: Chosen for a single objective, low-maintenance machine standard. Accepted cost: the clipboard behaviour and per-state visual distinctness named in AC8 are left without automated witness.

nodes.title: Fake-clock expiry harness
nodes.body: Constructs the backend with a controllable fake clock. The harness can set an absolute instant, advance beyond a drop's 24-hour default expiry, and assert behaviour on both sides of the boundary. Runs inside npm test with no timers patched globally.

nodes.title: Request recorder harness
nodes.body: Test-only middleware mounted ahead of the API routes. Records, per request: method, path, query string, headers, and raw body bytes before any parsing. Exposes the recorded log to assertions and is never mounted in production startup.

nodes.title: Plaintext sentinel sweep
nodes.body: Defines a high-entropy sentinel string used as file content and note text, then searches for it across three surfaces after an upload: the SQLite database file and all table values as raw bytes, captured server log output, and every request recorded by the request recorder harness. The sweep searches for the sentinel in plain, base64, and hex encodings so an incidental encoding does not hide a leak. The sentinel value itself is defined by the check.

nodes.title: Real Web Crypto envelope suite
nodes.body: Node-environment Vitest suite exercising the crypto envelope module against Node's webcrypto: key generation, AES-GCM-256 seal with the five AAD fields bound per D3, open, and deliberate corruption of ciphertext, nonce, and individual AAD fields. No mocking of SubtleCrypto.

nodes.title: Drop API integration suite
nodes.body: Drives the Drop API in-process against a temporary SQLite database: upload, retrieve, revoke, and rejection paths. Asserts status codes, response bodies, and resulting database state, including that no row is created on rejected uploads. Composes with the fake-clock and request-recorder harnesses.

nodes.title: Automated accessibility scan
nodes.body: Renders a view in jsdom, runs axe-core against the resulting DOM, and fails on any violation of serious or critical impact. Applied to the sender view, the recipient view, and the shared shell in both routes.

nodes.title: Check: sentinel absent from database, logs, and recorded requests
nodes.body: Upload a drop whose file content and note are the sentinel. Then assert the sentinel appears nowhere in the SQLite file bytes, nowhere in captured log output, and nowhere in any recorded request body, header, or query string, in plain, base64, or hex encoding. Passing evidence: three empty match sets.

nodes.title: Check: byte-identical round trip through the real envelope
nodes.body: Seal a binary fixture and a note with real AES-GCM-256, transport the envelope through the Drop API, then open it with the recipient-side key. Assert the recovered bytes equal the original byte-for-byte and the note string is exactly equal. Passing evidence: byte-array equality and string equality.

nodes.title: Check: retrieval after expiry returns 404 or 410 with no ciphertext
nodes.body: Create a drop at a fixed fake instant, confirm retrieval succeeds before expiry, advance the fake clock past 24 hours, then retrieve again. Assert status is 404 or 410 and the response body contains no ciphertext, nonce, or metadata field. Passing evidence: status assertion plus absence of envelope fields in the response.

nodes.title: Check: revocation deletes the drop and the recipient link cannot revoke
nodes.body: Revoke using the raw revocation token, asserting the server matched it against the stored SHA-256 hash. Assert subsequent retrieval returns 404 or 410. Separately attempt revocation using only values derivable from the recipient link and assert it is rejected while the drop remains retrievable. Passing evidence: both status assertions and unchanged drop state after the failed attempt.

nodes.title: Check: tampered ciphertext, nonce, or AAD field causes open to throw
nodes.body: For each of ciphertext, nonce, and each of the five AAD fields independently, mutate one byte or value and attempt to open the envelope. Assert every attempt throws and returns no partial plaintext. Passing evidence: a thrown error per mutation case and no plaintext bytes produced.

nodes.title: Check: upload of 10 MB + 1 byte returns 413 and creates no row
nodes.body: POST a payload one byte over the 10 MB ceiling. Assert the response status is 413 and that the drops table row count is unchanged. Passing evidence: status assertion plus before/after row count equality.

nodes.title: Check: key material absent from every recorded request
nodes.body: Complete a full sender-then-recipient cycle. For every request captured by the recorder, assert the decryption key material appears in no path, query string, header, or body. Passing evidence: an empty match set across the whole recorded log. Known limitation: a server-side view cannot distinguish deliberate fragment discipline from browser behaviour.

nodes.title: Check: sender and recipient views pass an axe-core scan
nodes.body: Render the sender view (including result state with recipient and revocation links) and the recipient view, then run axe-core against each. Assert zero violations of serious or critical impact. Passing evidence: empty serious/critical violation lists. Does not witness AC8's clipboard behaviour or per-state visual distinctness.

nodes.title: Check: secure-terminal shell passes an axe-core scan on both routes
nodes.body: Render the shared shell as mounted on the sender route and on the recipient route, run axe-core against each, and assert zero violations of serious or critical impact. Passing evidence: empty serious/critical violation lists for both routes.

nodes.title: Clipboard stub harness
nodes.body: Replaces navigator.clipboard with a recording stub in the jsdom test environment. Captures every writeText call in order and exposes the captured values to assertions. No real clipboard access, no permissions prompt, no external dependency.

nodes.title: Check: copy controls write the exact recipient and revocation links
nodes.body: Render the sender result state for a completed drop. Activate the recipient-link copy control and assert the clipboard stub captured the recipient share link exactly, including its URL fragment. Activate the revocation-link copy control and assert the stub captured the revocation link exactly. Assert the two captured values differ and that the recipient value is never written by the revocation control. Passing evidence: two exact string matches in the expected order, and inequality between them.

nodes.title: Secure terminal shell (shared UI)
nodes.body:
The chrome that both sender and recipient views mount inside, giving the application one visual identity.

Responsibilities:
- Page frame: single centred column, monospace type scale, fixed dark terminal palette, visible application name (Wisp per D9).
- Landmark structure: one banner, one main, one status region for transient messages, so axe-core has a well-formed document on every route (AC9).
- Focus management: predictable tab order, always-visible focus indicator, focus moved to the status region when an operation completes or fails.
- Text rendering boundary: exposes a text-only rendering primitive for untrusted strings (filenames, notes) that never interprets markup, keeping CON7 enforceable in one place instead of at every call site.
- Styling boundary: owns the shared CSS module and the design tokens; MOD3 and MOD4 compose its classes rather than redefining colour, spacing, or type (D7).

Explicit non-responsibilities: no crypto, no network, no routing decisions, no knowledge of drop semantics.

nodes.title: Interaction state contract
nodes.body:
The finite set of states every interactive control in the shell must be able to express, each carrying a distinct CSS-module class so state is observable in the DOM rather than only visually.

States:
- idle — default, actionable
- hover / focus-visible — pointer and keyboard affordance, never collapsed into one another
- busy — operation in flight; control is non-actionable and announces progress
- success — operation completed; used for a completed copy action
- error — operation failed; paired with a message in the status region
- disabled — not actionable and not focusable, with a stated reason

Rules:
- No two states share a class name.
- Recipient-share and revocation link controls are visually distinguished from each other in every state, since confusing them is the destructive mistake (AC8).
- Colour is never the only channel distinguishing a state.

nodes.title: Traffic-capture oracle spans two surfaces with distinct claims
nodes.body:
Verification of traffic uses two recorders, each authoritative for different claims.

- Server-side request recorder (per D11): authoritative for what the service received and could have persisted. Subject of AC1.
- Client-side outbound-request spy: authoritative for what application code attempted to send. Subject of AC7.

No claim about key-material discipline may rest on the server-side surface alone, because the platform strips the fragment before transmission and would make such a claim pass unconditionally.

detail.chosen_option: Both surfaces, with each acceptance criterion assigned to the surface that can actually falsify it.
rejected: Server-side recorder alone (D11) — makes AC7 pass by platform behaviour rather than application correctness.
Client-side spy alone — cannot substantiate AC1's persistence claim about what reached the server.
Leaving CH7's limitation documented and unaddressed — acceptable but leaves the goal G2 defended by a check that cannot fail for the right reason.
detail.rationale: AC1 and AC7 make claims about different subjects: one about what arrived and persisted, one about what was attempted. A single oracle surface cannot falsify both.

nodes.title: Client outbound-request spy
nodes.body:
Wraps the outbound request function used by the frontend in the jsdom test environment and records every attempted request in order: method, full URL including query string, all headers, and the body serialized to a searchable form (string, or bytes decoded for scanning).

Properties:
- Records attempts, including any request a server would reject or never see.
- Scans recorded material for a given secret in plain, base64url, base64, and hex encodings, and in percent-encoded form, so a re-encoded leak is still caught.
- Requires the frontend to obtain its request function through a single injectable seam so the spy has one place to attach.

nodes.title: Check: no request initiated by the application carries key material
nodes.body:
Drive a complete cycle through the frontend: sender generates a key, encrypts, uploads, and produces links; recipient consumes a link, fetches, and decrypts.

Assertions:
- For every request recorded by the outbound-request spy, the key material appears in no URL path, no query string, no header value, and no body — in any of the scanned encodings.
- The recipient flow issues at least one request, so the empty-log case cannot pass vacuously.
- Positive control: with a deliberately leaky stub that appends the key to the request URL, the same assertion fails. This proves the oracle has teeth.

Passing evidence: empty match set across a non-empty recorded log, plus a demonstrated failure under the leaky stub.

nodes.title: UI acceptance uses two standards: accessibility scan plus state-contract assertion
nodes.body:
Automated UI acceptance rests on two standards, neither sufficient alone:

- Accessibility: axe-core scan with zero serious or critical violations (retained from D13).
- State structure: assertions that the rendered DOM honours the interaction state contract (API2).

Still not adopted: DOM snapshots, and any standard that judges visual appearance rather than structure. Nothing here claims the interface looks good — only that its states are structurally distinguishable.

detail.chosen_option: Accessibility scan plus structural assertion against the enumerated state contract.
rejected: axe-core alone (D13) — leaves AC8's distinctness clause with no witness.
DOM snapshots — brittle and assert incidental markup rather than the contract.
Visual regression imaging — requires a browser engine, conflicting with CON8 and CON9.
Manual checklist — not machine-verified.
detail.rationale: API2 made distinctness a stated, finite contract; a structural assertion against it can now fail for the right reason. Appearance remains deliberately unjudged.

nodes.title: State-contract assertion harness
nodes.body:
Renders a shell control in jsdom, drives it into each state enumerated by API2 through the same inputs a user or operation would supply, and reads back the class list applied at each state.

Properties:
- Reads applied classes from the rendered DOM, not from the CSS-module import, so a class defined but never applied fails.
- Compares class sets across states and across control variants.
- Asserts nothing about colour, spacing, or rendered pixels.

nodes.title: Check: rendered controls honour the interaction state contract
nodes.body:
For each interactive control in the shell:

- Every state enumerated by API2 that the control supports applies at least one class distinct from its idle state.
- No two states of the same control apply identical class sets; hover and focus-visible in particular are not collapsed.
- Disabled controls are non-focusable in the rendered DOM, not merely styled as disabled.

For the sender result view specifically:
- The recipient-share control and the revocation control never share an identical class set in any state.

Passing evidence: a per-state class map with no duplicate entries, distinct maps for the two link controls, and a disabled control absent from the focus order.
